anchors.paper_title: Cross-modal interaction of Alpha Activity does not reflect inhibition of early sensory processing: A frequency tagging study using EEG and MEG
anchors.reason: Same authors and paradigm (cross-modal cue, 36 Hz visual and 40 Hz auditory frequency tagging); the eLife study reports the EEG/MEG data in this CrossModal dataset.

metadata.methods_description: Participants performed a cross-modal target-discrimination task in which cues indicated whether an upcoming target would be auditory (tone) or visual (Gabor patch/disc). During the cue-target interval (3 seconds), a fixation cross was frequency-tagged at 36 Hz while an amplitude-modulated 40 Hz tone was played. In Block 1, targets were presented without distractors; in Block 2, targets were accompanied by a distractor from the other sensory modality. Stimulus difficulty was individually calibrated for auditory and visual conditions prior to the main experiment. Eye-tracking (eye-link) data were also collected to monitor eye movements during MEG recording. One participant (sub-07) was excluded due to incomplete data collection and poor performance.

citation_details.title: Opposite Effects of Alpha Oscillations on Mind-Wandering with Eyes Open and Closed
citation_details.author: Esther M Thielking, Hannah Ramsey, Jason Samaha, Thomas Andrillon, Luca Iemi
citation_details.abstract: Spontaneous fluctuations in brain activity are thought to underlie mind-wandering, moments when mental experience becomes unrelated to what one is currently doing. A large body of research has investigated ongoing neural oscillations in the alpha band (7-14 Hz), reflecting changes in arousal and attention. However, studies disagree whether the power of alpha oscillations increases or decreases during mind-wandering compared with on-task focus. We hypothesized that these opposite effects arise from differences in eye state across studies, as eye closure increases alpha power and can reverse alpha's relationship with sleepiness, which is itself related to mind-wandering. citation_details.title: Temporal Structure of Item Presentation Modulates Brain Oscillations in Verbal Working Memory
citation_details.author: Alexandra I. Kosachenko, Danil I. Syttykov, Dmitry Tarasov, Alexander I. Kotyusov, Dauren Kasanov, Sergey B. Malykh, Boris Kotchoubey, Yuri G. Pavlov
citation_details.abstract: Previous studies of verbal working memory (WM) have reported inconsistent changes in alpha power during retention, with both increases and decreases observed. We asked whether these discrepancies arise from how stimuli are presented. Thirty adults memorized seven digits presented in four modes: Simultaneous (all digits for 2800 ms) or sequential presentations at Fast (400 ms per digit), Slow (1000 ms per digit), and Fast + delay (400 ms per digit plus a 600-ms free time in between). We analyzed EEG during encoding and a 6-s retention period in theta (4-7 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), and beta (18-24 Hz) frequency bands. Encoding produced parametric load-related theta increase and beta decrease, possibly reflecting growing executive control demands and motor program formation, respectively. citation_details.title: OPM quantum sensors enhance non-invasive neuroimaging performance
citation_details.author: Marion Brickwedde, Paul Anders, P. Krüger, Tilmann H. Sander, Peter J. Uhlhaas
citation_details.abstract: Much of our understanding of how neural circuit activity relates to human behaviour as well as mental health stems from non-invasive assessments of the central nervous system. Further progress in key questions, however, requires a higher differentiation of circuit-level activity, which remains constrained by the sensitivity and resolution of existing instruments. Here we show that neural quantum sensing with optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) addresses this issue by significantly outperforming EEG and conventional MEG in both signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and signal coherence across trials. SNR for OPMs was increased by up to 205% compared to EEG and by up to 40% compared to conventional MEG. Likewise, the signal coherence across trials of OPMs was increased by up to 61% compared to EEG and by up to 23% compared to conventional MEG.
